Attrition means the slow, gradual process of wearing something down — reducing its strength, size, or numbers — through continuous pressure, friction, or repeated loss over time.

Think of a river and a rock. If you drop a rock into a still pond, nothing happens to it. But if that same rock sits in a flowing river for thousands of years, the constant, steady movement of water grinds it down, smooths it out, and makes it smaller and smaller. That grinding-down process is the soul of attrition.

The qualities that define attrition in every context are:

  • It is slow and gradual — never sudden or explosive
  • It is cumulative — each small loss adds up to a big one over time
  • It is caused by continuous, sustained pressure or repeated action
  • The end result is depletion, weakening, or disappearance

1. The Physical/Literal Meaning — Wearing Down by Friction

In its most concrete sense, attrition is the physical wearing away of a surface or object through rubbing and friction.

Rocks tumbling against each other in a river gradually become smaller, rounder, and smoother through attrition. In dentistry, dental attrition refers to the wearing down of tooth enamel from grinding your teeth over many years.

This physical sense is the original, root meaning — and understanding it makes every other meaning click into place.

2. The Military Meaning — Wearing Down an Enemy

This is one of the most important and widely used senses of the word. In warfare, attrition is the strategy of gradually depleting the enemy's soldiers, weapons, supplies, and morale through relentless, continuous fighting — rather than trying to defeat them in a single decisive strike.

The idea is: even if you cannot overpower the enemy in one blow, you can grind them down over time until they are too exhausted and depleted to fight on.

The phrase you will encounter most is "a war of attrition" — a conflict where both sides keep battering each other, suffering losses, and wearing each other out, with no quick resolution in sight.

The clearest real-world example is World War I (1914–1918). Both sides dug into trenches and fought for years, not with bold breakthroughs, but in a grinding, devastating back-and-forth. Neither side won quickly — they simply eroded each other's capacity to fight.

3. The Business and HR Meaning — Loss of Employees Over Time

In business and human resources (HR), attrition means the gradual shrinking of a workforce as employees leave over time — through resignation, retirement, or death — without being replaced.

This is importantly different from being fired or laid off. Attrition is the organic, natural loss of people from an organization, not an active decision to remove them.

You will often hear "natural attrition" — the idea of letting staff numbers fall on their own as people leave. A company facing financial trouble might say: "We will reduce our headcount through natural attrition" — meaning: we won't fire anyone, but when people resign or retire, we simply won't hire replacements.

"Attrition rate" (also called "employee attrition rate") is a number companies track — it tells you what percentage of the workforce left the company within a given time period. A high attrition rate is usually a warning sign that something is wrong.

4. The Broader, Everyday Meaning — Gradual Reduction of Anything

Beyond warfare and business, attrition is used widely to describe the slow erosion of anything — enthusiasm, customer loyalty, public support, a group's membership, or even one's beliefs.

  • Customer attrition: Customers gradually stop using a product or service over time. You may also hear this called "churn."
  • Student attrition: Students who drop out of a course or school without completing it.
  • Political attrition: Public support for a leader or movement slowly fading away over time.

The word works wherever something is being slowly drained, worn down, or reduced — not in a dramatic moment, but quietly, steadily, over time.

5. The Theological Meaning (Specialized)

This meaning is rare outside of religious study, but worth knowing. In Catholic theology, attrition means imperfect contrition — feeling sorry for your sins primarily out of fear of punishment, rather than out of genuine love of God. It is considered a lesser, weaker form of repentance compared to true contrition, which comes from love. You are unlikely to encounter this meaning in everyday reading unless you are studying religion specifically.
The Most Important Phrase: "War of Attrition"

Even outside of actual warfare, people use "war of attrition" figuratively to describe any long, drawn-out struggle where both sides are simply trying to outlast each other.

"The legal battle between the two rival companies became a war of attrition — both had spent millions in legal fees and neither was willing to back down."

You will see this phrase used in politics, sports, business rivalries, negotiations, and personal conflicts. Whenever a struggle is less about who is stronger and more about who can hold on longer, that is a war of attrition.

Attrition is not the same as turnover. In HR, turnover is a broader term that covers both people leaving and new people being hired to replace them. Attrition focuses specifically on the loss side — the net shrinking — without necessarily bringing in replacements.

Attrition is not a sudden event. If something ends abruptly and dramatically — a company collapses, an army surrenders overnight — that is not attrition. Attrition always creeps up on you. It is the enemy you do not notice until the damage is already done.

Attrition can be a deliberate strategy or an unintended outcome. Militaries can choose a strategy of attrition. But in business, education, or everyday life, attrition often just happens to you — it is something you observe and measure, not necessarily something you planned.

• "The tech company announced it would reduce its staff of 600 through attrition over the next two years, promising no forced layoffs."
  • "The protest movement slowly died not from any single defeat but through attrition — people gradually lost energy and stopped turning up."
  • "The two rival nations settled into a war of attrition, each side trying to outlast the other economically."
  • "The university president expressed concern over the high attrition rate among first-generation college students."
  • "Years of neglect led to the silent attrition of public trust in the institution."
  • "Teeth grinding at night causes dental attrition that can seriously damage your enamel over time."

Attrition is the slow, steady, and cumulative process of wearing something down — whether it is a rock, an army, a workforce, or a relationship — through continuous pressure, friction, or loss, until it is significantly weakened or gone.
